criterion_notes.c1: Examines household access to piped running water and adoption/reconstruction of standard-compliant household sanitary latrines (as well as wastewater canal and refuse collection infrastructure) as components of a rural primary health care project in Dahu, Fujian.
criterion_notes.c2: Passes the plain wording of Criterion 2 ('yes' -> plain_criterion2_decision: 'include'), because the study evaluates a multisectoral local-government institutional arrangement (a 14-member town planning committee, local public financing, a 100-yuan village latrine reconstruction subsidy, and a local ordinance requiring homes to separate the kitchen, toilet, and pigpen and build a toilet behind the house). Fails the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading ('no' -> decision: 'exclude', E03), because the evaluated exposure is an unbundled community primary health care (PHC) and behavioural health-education demonstration project ('Changes before and after Health Education Intervention'): piped water access (unserved share reduced from 16% to 5%) reflects pure physical network extension with no legal or regulatory mechanism, and the brief descriptive mention of a local housing/toilet ordinance and flat hardware construction grant within a village-wide hygiene promotion campaign does not empirically examine any rule-type access mechanism (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation/tenure requirements, utility tariff/cost-recovery rules, discretion, or enforcement).
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary empirical before-and-after evaluation data from a 1989 baseline household visit survey of all homes in the first two target hamlets and a 1-year follow-up evaluation (reporting pre-post percentages in text, although Table 1's cells are omitted in the PDF scan/text).
criterion_notes.c4: Reports household water and sanitation access outcomes in the two target hamlets: percentage of the population without access to running water (reduced from 16% to 5%), percentage of households with a sanitary latrine conforming to state standards (0% to 15%), and percentage of homes separating kitchen, pigpen, and toilet (7% to 60%).
criterion_notes.c5: Identifies the population (households/residents in two target hamlets of Dahu Village, Yongan County, Fujian), the bundled exposure (Year-1 multisectoral PHC and health education intervention), the outcomes (running water access and compliant latrine/toilet separation rates), and the study design (uncontrolled pre-post community intervention evaluation), though exact sample sizes for the two hamlets are not reported and individual legal/subsidy components are not separated from health education and construction.

evidence_quotes.quote: At the beginning of the project 16% of the population in the two hamlets did not have access to running water. At the end of the project’s first year this figure was reduced to 5% through the extension of the piped water system to all houses except three that are far from the center of the hamlets.

The percentage of households that have a latrine that conforms to the new standards has risen from 0 to 15%. Reluctance to reconstruct latrines is attributed to the fact that the 100 yuan supplement provided by the village government is estimated to cover less than half the actual cost.

an ordinance was passed that any new homes constructed must meet the requirement of separating the kitchen, toilet, and pigpen. They are also required to have a backyard garden, and a toilet built behind the house according to the above guidelines. Homes built prior to the adoption of the ordinances were given a specified amount of time to make the corrections.
Table 1. Household Sanitation Practices. Changes before and after Health Education Intervention, Dahu Village, Fujian Province, China
A baseline survey was conducted in the first two target hamlets. All homes were visited by a health worker who recorded the practice of various hygienic behaviors.

raw_response.exposure: Multisectoral primary health care (PHC) and health education demonstration program combining community hygiene education, piped water and sewage canal construction, a 100-yuan household latrine reconstruction subsidy, local housing/sanitation ordinances, and clinic upgrades
raw_response.outcome: Percentage of population without access to running water (16% at baseline to 5% at Year 1); percentage of households with a sanitary latrine conforming to new standards (0% to 15%); percentage of homes separating kitchen, pigpen, and toilet (7% to 60%)
raw_response.population_and_sample: Households and residents in the first two target hamlets of Dahu Village, Yongan County, Fujian Province, China (total Dahu population is 18,600 across 18 hamlets; all homes in the first two target hamlets were visited at baseline in 1989, exact hamlet sample size not reported)
raw_response.rationale: Excluded as E03 (Wrong exposure) under the 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading of Criterion 2, while qualifying as 'include' under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2. The paper reports 1-year pre-post evaluation findings from two rural hamlets in Dahu, Fujian, China, for a multisectoral Primary Health Care (PHC) and health education demonstration project. Although it reports water and sanitation access outcomes (unserved piped-water share falling from 16% to 5% and compliant sanitary latrine coverage rising from 0% to 15%) and passes plain Criterion 2 by describing intersectoral village committee governance, a local housing ordinance on separating toilets from kitchens/pigpens, and a 100-yuan village latrine subsidy, it fails the narrow rule-type Criterion 2 scope: improved water access resulted purely from physical piped-network extension, and sanitation outcomes reflect an unbundled PHC health-education and infrastructure delivery package without empirical analysis of any rule-type mechanism governing service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, tenure/documentation requirements, utility tariff/cost-recovery rules, discretion, or enforcement).
raw_response.study_design: Uncontrolled before-and-after (pre-post) community demonstration program evaluation
